Baby & Child

Surgery for an undescended testicle: a guide for parents

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

An undescended testicle has not reached its usual position in the scrotum. Some descend during early infancy, but continued waiting is not always appropriate. If surgery is needed, the operation to move and secure the testicle in the scrotum is called orchidopexy, also spelled orchiopexy.

Arrange assessment at the right time

Testicles are checked during newborn and later child-health examinations. If a testicle has not descended by six months of corrected age, referral to a surgical specialist is recommended. Corrected age takes prematurity into account.

The aim is generally to complete treatment early: European guidance recommends surgery between six and twelve months where possible, and by eighteen months at the latest. If an older child is newly found to have a high testicle, they also need referral rather than assuming the opportunity for treatment has passed.

A retractile testicle, which can move up with a muscle reflex but can be brought down and remain temporarily, is different from an undescended testicle. It usually needs regular checks rather than immediate surgery. Let a clinician make that distinction; do not repeatedly pull or manipulate it at home.

If neither testicle can be felt in a newborn, prompt specialist assessment is needed, sometimes including hormone or genetic investigations. Do not simply wait until the usual six-month referral point.

The testicles develop in the abdomen before birth and usually move into the scrotum during pregnancy. Descent can still occur in the first few months, especially after premature birth, but an examination should track progress. Published percentages differ by population and should not be used to justify waiting beyond the recommended referral period.

Why surgery may be recommended

The scrotum provides a cooler environment for the testicles. Leaving a testicle undescended can affect its development and future sperm production. The implications are generally greater when both testicles are affected.

An undescended testicle is also associated with an increased risk of testicular cancer and may occur with a groin hernia. Early treatment helps address these concerns and makes the testicle easier to examine later.

Surgery cannot promise normal fertility or completely remove the additional cancer risk. Equally, an undescended testicle does not mean your child will be infertile or develop cancer. The specialist can discuss the outlook for the position and condition of your child’s testicle.

The operation is planned around the testicle’s location

The surgeon first examines your child. An ultrasound is not routinely needed before referral because it may not reliably locate a testicle or change the initial plan. Additional investigations are selected for particular circumstances.

A testicle felt in the groin can often be moved through a small groin or scrotal incision. The surgeon frees the surrounding tissues, preserves the blood supply and sperm-carrying duct, and secures the testicle in the scrotum. A related hernia may be repaired at the same time.

If the testicle cannot be felt, examination under anaesthetic and keyhole surgery may be needed to find it. A higher abdominal testicle may need a different operation, sometimes performed in two stages several months apart.

Occasionally the surgeon finds a testicle or remnant that has not developed or has lost its blood supply. Removal may be advised. Discuss these possibilities during consent, including what the surgeon would do if the findings differ from those expected.

In a typical groin operation, the surgeon releases attachments around the spermatic cord so the testicle can reach the scrotum without excess tension. The cord carries blood vessels and the vas deferens, the tube that carries sperm. The cremaster muscle and a developmental attachment called the gubernaculum may be involved in this anatomy; the exact dissection depends on the testicle’s location. A small scrotal pocket is made and the testicle is secured there.

Preparing your child and asking questions

The operation is usually performed under general anaesthesia. Follow the hospital’s precise instructions about when to stop food, milk and clear fluids; these do not all necessarily have the same cut-off time.

Tell the team about medicines, allergies and any new illness before surgery. They will explain how anaesthesia will be started, pain relief and whether you can stay while your child goes to sleep.

For a child old enough to understand, use simple language about going to hospital and having a sore area afterwards. A familiar toy and a chance to ask questions may help. Feeling worried yourself is understandable and is not something to feel guilty about.

Ask whether this is expected to be a day-case procedure, whether another stage may be needed and whom to contact if problems occur after discharge.

Anaesthesia may begin through a mask or an intravenous cannula, depending on the plan. A cannula is often placed in the hand, arm or foot, sometimes after the child is asleep. The anaesthetist monitors breathing and other vital signs throughout. Afterwards, recovery staff observe the child until it is safe for you to rejoin them and for discharge to be considered.

Recovery needs an individual plan

Many children go home the same day once they have recovered sufficiently from anaesthesia, can drink and are comfortable. Some need a longer stay because of their age, medical needs or the procedure performed.

Bruising and some swelling can occur. Give the pain relief recommended by the team, using the correct dose and interval for your child. Do not wait until pain is severe if regular doses have been advised.

Follow the instructions for wound cleaning, bathing, nappies and dressings. Stitches are often dissolvable, but the team will confirm this. Avoid applying creams or antiseptics unless advised.

Plan quiet activities at first. Cycling, straddle toys, rough play and sports may need to wait longer. Published hospital instructions differ substantially according to procedure, so use your surgeon’s dates for nursery, school, swimming and sport instead of a universal one-month rule.

Know the risks and keep follow-up appointments

Possible complications include bleeding, infection, damage to the sperm-carrying duct, loss of blood supply with shrinkage of the testicle, or the testicle moving up again. The risk varies with its original position and the operation required. These are part of informed consent, not risks to dismiss as negligible.

Contact the surgical team promptly for increasing redness, heat, discharge from the wound, fever, uncontrolled pain, persistent vomiting or difficulty passing urine. Sudden severe testicular or groin pain needs emergency assessment, even after a previous orchidopexy.

Follow-up checks assess the wound, position and growth of the testicle. Around puberty, the clinician can explain testicular awareness and self-examination appropriate to this history. New lumps or changes should be checked.

If an undescended testicle is first recognised after puberty, management is different and individualised. Removal is sometimes recommended, but age alone does not prove that the tissue has no function. A urologist considers the other testicle, fertility goals and overall risks.

Anaesthetic reactions, bleeding, infection and significant pain are also discussed during consent. If both testicles are absent or have little function, a paediatric hormone specialist may be needed to plan later development and long-term care. Follow-up should clarify this rather than assuming the operation solves every hormonal concern.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Specialist urology guidance recommends early referral and surgery when spontaneous descent has not occurred, with timing adjusted for prematurity and local pathways.

Aftercare and activity restrictions depend on the operation; follow the surgical team’s written instructions and attend follow-up.

How BeMama can help

Bring questions about location, one- or two-stage surgery, anaesthesia, activity and long-term testicular health to the consent appointment.

When to seek help

Both testicles not palpable in a newborn warrants prompt specialist assessment; sudden severe scrotal pain, inability to urinate or worsening illness after surgery needs urgent care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • An undescended testicle still present at six months corrected age needs specialist referral.
  • Early surgery is recommended when spontaneous descent has not occurred.
  • The operation depends on whether the testicle is in the groin, abdomen or not found.
  • Recovery instructions vary with the procedure.
  • Keep follow-up appointments because surgery does not remove every future risk.

Frequently asked questions

Will my child always need two operations?

No. Many groin testicles can be treated in one operation. Some higher abdominal testicles need a staged approach.

Does surgery eliminate the risk of testicular cancer?

No. Early treatment can reduce risk and makes examination easier, but the history remains relevant later in life.

Should I request an ultrasound before the specialist visit?

Usually not. Examination and referral come first; the specialist decides whether any imaging would help.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
